title: New York State Comptroller
area: Statewide — all of New York State

context.text: Incumbent Thomas P. DiNapoli won the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary against Drew Warshaw and Raj Goyle, 65.7% to 20.1% to 13.8% (of 878,117 votes cast) — his first contested primary since taking office in 2007.

The Working Families Party's June 2026 primary was won by Sienna Fontaine, but Ballotpedia's general-election candidate listing shows DiNapoli, not Fontaine, holding the Working Families Party ballot line in November; reporting from May 2026 noted the party had the option to substitute its nominee before a July deadline and that Fontaine had not campaigned for the office.
The Republican and Conservative Party primaries were canceled; Joseph Hernandez was unopposed and received the Republican State Committee's nomination at its convention.
A September 2026 Siena University poll of likely voters found DiNapoli leading Hernandez 56% to 33%, with 12% undecided (margin of error ±3.9%).

candidates.name: Thomas P. DiNapoli
candidates.ballotNote: Won the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary with 65.7% against Drew Warshaw and Raj Goyle.

summary.text: Thomas P. DiNapoli is the incumbent Democratic State Comptroller, seeking a fifth full term. A lifelong Long Islander who first won public office at 18 on a school board, he served 20 years in the State Assembly before the Legislature chose him as Comptroller in February 2007; voters elected him in 2010, 2014, 2018 and 2022. He oversees the $300-billion-plus New York State Common Retirement Fund, conducts audits of state agencies and local governments, and manages the state's finances. He won the June 2026 Democratic primary and campaigned on the fund's growth and financial health, opposing Governor Hochul's proposal to raise the dollar threshold for his office's review of state contracts.

background.text: Describes himself as a lifelong Long Islander raised in a middle-class, union household; born in 1954 in Rockville Centre and raised in Albertson, per Wikipedia.

Earned a bachelor's degree in history from Hofstra University (magna cum laude, 1976); worked in the telecommunications industry for about ten years while taking night classes toward a master's degree from The New School University's Graduate School of Management and Urban Professions.

Elected at 17 in 1972 as a trustee of the Mineola Union Free School District Board of Education and took office at 18, reportedly the youngest person to hold public office in New York at the time; served until 1982.

Elected to the New York State Assembly in 1986 and represented the 16th District in northwestern Nassau County for 20 years, until 2007; chaired the Environmental Conservation, Local Governments and Governmental Operations committees, per Wikipedia.

Elected State Comptroller by a bipartisan majority of the State Legislature on February 7, 2007, to fill the vacancy created when Alan Hevesi resigned in December 2006 and pleaded guilty to a fraud charge.
Elected Comptroller by voters in 2010, 2014, 2018 and 2022; Wikipedia notes he received more votes than any other statewide candidate in 2014 and 2018.

Oversees the New York State Common Retirement Fund; his official biography describes his work on fighting fraud, saying it has resulted in hundreds of arrests and tens of millions of dollars in restitution, and on steps to protect the pension fund from climate-related investment risk.
Received the Democratic nomination for a fifth full term in February 2026 and won the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary with 65.7% of the vote over Drew Warshaw and Raj Goyle.

priorities.text: Continuing to grow the state pension fund, which he says reached a record $309.7 billion and is about 97% funded, calling it 'virtually a fully funded public pension plan.'
priorities.quote: We are 97% funded, so we're virtually a fully funded public pension plan.

priorities.text: Addressing affordability, citing the cost pressures New York families face and pointing to the fund's role in investments in health care, housing and education.
Maintaining independent oversight of state contracts and spending, opposing a 2026 budget proposal to raise the threshold for his office's contract review from $50,000 to $300,000.

positions.summary: Set a 2040 net-zero emissions target for the pension fund and in February 2024 restricted investment in eight oil and gas companies found not "transition-ready," while continuing to hold most major oil and gas companies, including the bulk of its ExxonMobil position, after determining they met minimum transition standards.

record.text: Reported the New York State Common Retirement Fund valued at $309.7 billion at the end of the first quarter of State Fiscal Year 2026-27 (as of June 30, 2026), with an estimated 6.12% quarterly return and a 96.8% funded status.

Reported the pension fund posted an 11.94% annual return for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, closing at a then-record $295.4 billion; the fund's report cited a 92.2% funded status as of the prior fiscal year-end (March 31, 2025), with the new year's status still being calculated.

Released an independent fiduciary review by Weaver and Tidwell LLP, the fund's fifth statutorily required review (covering April 2021–March 2024), which found the fund operates with the highest ethical standards and in full compliance with fiduciary and statutory requirements, while making five recommendations for process improvements.

Released a follow-up and new round of state agency audits on July 29, 2026, finding the Department of Health made little progress addressing prior Medicaid program recommendations, that Medicaid laboratory services had $21.6 million in improper payments due to inadequate provider guidance, and citing oversight weaknesses at the Office for People With Developmental Disabilities and the Empire State Plaza Performing Arts Center.

Released an audit finding the Department of Environmental Conservation cannot reliably measure how much waste is recycled statewide: DEC did not receive 341 of 1,065 required annual reports from recycling facilities over a three-year period, and 35% of registered and permitted facilities were not inspected.

Announced in February 2024 that the pension fund would restrict investment in eight integrated oil and gas companies, including ExxonMobil, determined not to be "transition-ready" to a low-carbon economy, divesting corporate bonds and actively managed public equity holdings worth about $26.8 million.

candidates.name: Joseph Hernandez
candidates.ballotNote: Nominated by the Republican State Committee at its convention; the Republican and Conservative primaries were canceled as he was unopposed.

summary.text: Joseph Hernandez is the Republican and Conservative Party nominee for Comptroller, running against incumbent Thomas DiNapoli. Born in Cuba and a self-described former refugee, he is a biotechnology entrepreneur and investment-firm executive who has not previously held elected office; he ran as an independent candidate for New York City mayor in 2025 before entering the comptroller race. His campaign centers on auditing state spending, creating a fraud task force, and increasing upstate economic investment.

background.text: Born in Camagüey, Cuba, per his Ballotpedia survey; according to his campaign website, he fled communist rule at age seven and arrived in the United States, and describes his father as a political prisoner.

According to his campaign website, he attended Florida public schools and earned a B.S. in neuroscience, an M.S. in molecular genetics and microbiology, and an MBA in finance and entrepreneurship, all from the University of Florida.

Earned an M.S. in chronic disease epidemiology and biostatistics from Yale University; his campaign website lists a master's in global healthcare leadership from the University of Oxford, which a November 2025 news report described as still in progress.
According to his campaign website, his career began at Merck & Co. and continued at Affymetrix and then Digene Corp., a maker of an FDA-approved HPV test that was acquired by Qiagen.

Says he has founded, invested in and led more than a dozen biotechnology, healthcare and technology companies, and is Founder and Senior Managing Partner of the biotech investment firm Blue Water Venture Partners.
Ran as an independent candidate for Mayor of New York City in the November 2025 general election on the Quality of Life Party line, receiving about 0.1% of the vote (1,379 votes).

Announced his run for State Comptroller in November 2025 and was nominated unanimously by the Republican State Committee at its convention in Garden City in early 2026; he also appears on the Conservative Party line.
According to his campaign website, he is the father of three children.

priorities.text: Conducting real-time audits of every state agency and public authority to catch waste, fraud and mismanagement faster.
priorities.quote: Right now, we find out about malfeasance and people stealing taxpayer dollars years out. That's not acceptable.

priorities.text: Creating a dedicated Fraud Strike Task Force to identify suspicious payment patterns and refer cases to law enforcement, with pre-payment fraud detection to stop improper payments before they go out.
Strengthening pension fund performance and cutting what he describes as excessive Wall Street investment fees.
priorities.quote: Every unnecessary dollar paid in investment fees is a dollar that is not working for New York retirees.

priorities.text: Creating a $10 billion "Empire Opportunity Fund" to attract investment in manufacturing, technology, energy, life sciences and logistics, with emphasis on upstate and western New York.
Opposing a 2026 executive budget proposal to raise the state contract-review threshold from $50,000 to $300,000, which he has said he would sue to block.
priorities.quote: If that goes forward, then we will absolutely follow a suit the next day after that occurs.

positions.summary: Says New York has a spending problem rather than a revenue shortfall and campaigns on auditing and reining in state spending rather than raising taxes.

candidates.researchNotes: Hernandez has not previously held elected office, so there is no voting or official-action record to list. His positions on issues outside the comptroller's fiscal and oversight mandate (e.g. abortion, guns, immigration) were not found in campaign materials or press coverage as of this research.

researchNotes: FEC/federal campaign-finance data is not applicable to this state office. This is a state-office record, so the brief's federal-incumbent finance/vote carve-out does not apply, but no official campaign-finance totals were independently verified beyond what Ballotpedia's finance summaries show; readers should consult the state Board of Elections for current filings. Hernandez's biography relies largely on his own campaign materials and Ballotpedia survey; no independent news profile confirming his employment history was found.
